#99026. There’s a Ton of Conspiracies About Lab-Grown Meat Right Now. Here’s What’s Really True.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1252 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

There’s a Ton of Conspiracies About Lab-Grown Meat Right Now. Here’s What’s Really True.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lab-grown meat is having an absolute field day on social media, as tons of outlandish claims and conspiracy theories about it are forming: The lab-grown industry is trying to sneak it into our grocery carts by labeling it as natural meat!
  • Formally known as cultivated meat, lab-grown meat has been in development for more than a decade, but it’s only recently begun to capture mainstream attention.
  • Meet the experts: Elliot Swartz, PhD, is a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lab-grown meat is having an absolute field day on social media, as tons of outlandish claims and conspiracy theories about it are forming: The lab-grown industry is trying to sneak it into our grocery carts by labeling it as natural meat! Here’s why you need to avoid it at all costs! In truth, there’s a lot more to the story, and a ton of those claims are false.

Formally known as cultivated meat, lab-grown meat has been in development for more than a decade, but it’s only recently begun to capture mainstream attention. In 2023, it received regulatory clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Now, it’s beginning to make its way into the market (albeit in limited quantities), says Steven Surico, RD, a registered dietitian with the Food and Nutrition Department at Good Samaritan University Hospital.

Meet the experts: Elliot Swartz, PhD, is a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute. Steven Surico, RD, is a registered dietitian with the Food and Nutrition Department at Good Samaritan University Hospital. Lauri Wright, RDN, is a registered dietitian and associate professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of South Florida College of Public Health.

Industry observers note that as such, lab-grown meat is becoming a grossly misunderstood concept. (Cue: The recent influx of misleading social media videos and AI-generated content.) These posts can blur the line between fact and fiction, leaving consumers unsure of what’s real, scaring them when there’s nothing to be afraid of. “The concern is that cultivated meat is something highly artificial, when in reality, it’s not,” states Surico.

Here’s everything you need to know about lab-grown meat, including what it is, whether it’s being sold in stores, and if you should truly worry about it, according to experts.

Cultivated meat is grown directly from animal cells, as opposed to natural meat that’s produced by raising and slaughtering an animal, says Elliot Swartz, PhD, a cultivated meat researcher and the senior principal scientist for cultivated meat at The Good Food Institute.

Industry observers note that “A small sample of cells is fed basic nutrients, like amino acids, fats, vitamins, salts, and sugars, in clean, controlled environments similar to those used to make yogurt, cheese, and beer, where the cells are grown and developed into meat or seafood,” he explains. As the cells multiply and develop, they form the muscle and other tissues that make up meat. Once mature, Swartz indicates they’re harvested and prepared as a product that should, at least in theory, offer the same taste, smell, texture, and consistency as ordinary meat.

Recent findings suggest that lab-grown meat vs. plant-based alternatives: “Beyond Meat products are made primarily from plant ingredients and do not contain animal muscle cells, whereas cultivated meat starts with animal cells and grows those cells into animal tissue,” Surico indicates.

In a recent development, cultivated meat may address some of the challenges associated with natural meat production, particularly when it comes to food safety, public health, nutrition, and the environmental impact of raising livestock. According to Swartz, one of the biggest advantages is the greater control over the production process, which could offer significant food safety benefits.

Industry observers note that research highlights that raising large populations of animals in close quarters can create opportunities for bacteria, other pathogens, and diseases to spread. This can increase the risk of transmission to humans through food (or animal) contact, but cultivated meat could help reduce these risks, Swartz explains.

Cultivated meat is also better for the environment by reducing the land, water, and greenhouse gas emissions needed for meat production. Research from The Good Food Institute even suggests that if cultivated meat can be produced commercially in large quantities using clean energy, it could have a significantly smaller environmental footprint than conventional meat.

In a recent development, finally, because the cells are grown in a controlled environment, researchers can influence the nutritional composition of the meat, indicates Lauri Wright, RDN, a registered dietitian and associate professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. For example, they can adjust the amount and types of fat in the meat to reduce saturated fat and cholesterol while increasing desirable nutrients like protein, she explains. Theoretically, this could lead to healthier meat that tastes the same, studies suggest.

While some people are afraid of lab-grown meat because they’re not really sure what’s in it, each product undergoes extensive testing by the FDA and USDA. So, its nutritional content is thoroughly tested to ensure it meets food safety standards, adds Swartz.

Yes, but availability is extremely limited. Cultivated meat has received approval from the FDA and USDA for sale in the U.S., as well as in Singapore and Australia, per The Good Food Institute. However, regulatory approval doesn’t necessarily mean that products are widely available. Plus, eight states in the U.S. have enacted bans or temporary restrictions on cultivated meat, including Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Mississippi, Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, and Texas. These restrictions are largely driven by concerns about protecting traditional agriculture and livestock industries.

So, contrary to what social media might have you believing, cultivated meat isn’t something you can pick up at your local supermarket just yet. In the U.S., the only products right now being served is Wildtype’s cultivated salmon at select restaurants in Washington D.C., Oregon, Arizona, and California and Upside Chicken at select restaurants in California.

In a recent development, while it’s difficult to predict exactly when lab-grown meat will be in grocery stores, Swartz expects a gradual rollout, with smaller, more specialized retailers being the first to carry it. “You could start to see cultivated meat products more widely introduced in higher-end retailers in the early 2030s, but I don’t think you’ll see it in big box grocery stores until the late 2030s,” he claims.

It has been revealed that in grocery stores, it’ll be clearly labeled as lab-grown or cultivated meat. “Due to the USDA regulations and labeling, it should be very clear to the consumer if they are buying regular meat or lab-grown meat,” indicates Surico. In fact, federal law prohibits food from being misbranded or carrying false or misleading labels, and regulators have remarked cultivated meat products must be clearly and accurately labeled.

As for the price, that remains to be seen. Cultivated meat is presently more expensive to produce than most conventional meat and seafood, but Swartz states the long-term goal is to bring production costs down to match or fall below those of conventional options.

Not very. “You should not be freaked out,” says Wright. “If anything, you should see it as potential, because the future of lab-grown meat could give consumers more options and alternatives to what they buy and put into their body.”.

In a recent development, swartz agrees, pointing out that the benefits go beyond offering another way to produce meat. “Whether you care about the environment, animal welfare, food safety, or public health, there’s a lot of potential benefits for cultivated meat that are additive in terms of value for the consumer,” he notes.

Of course, that doesn’t mean everyone has to embrace cultivated meat—traditional meat isn’t going away or being phased out of grocery stores or restaurants. The goal is simply to give consumers another option, not replace the foods they already know and enjoy. And if cultivated meat isn’t your jam, that’s perfectly fine, too.

  • I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast.
  • That excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few. As seen in this Sag Harbor home, this Parisian pied-à-terre, this Westchester residence, and this Connecticut country retreat, Mauviel is something of a status symbol in kitchens. Much like a Le Creuset Dutch oven out on display, spying a few copper pans from the French brand hanging from a rail signals that “Great Taste Lives Here.” And this week marks a good opportunity to join the club, with Mauviel sets and individual pieces up to 30% off for Black Friday at Williams Sonoma and on Shop.

I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast. Of course it does. Unlike some of my ceramic pans that catch and dry out an egg, the Mauviel has given me no trouble, delivering me the most perfect eggs to date I’ve ever cooked. Even against my stainless-steel pans (which I do love very much), these heat a bit more quickly and evenly.

That excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple. Mauviel has made copper cookware since 1830 in Villedieu-les-Poêles, a town in Normandy with an enduring history of copper manufacturing; the pieces are still handcrafted there. As far as their makeup, the M’150 B pieces are, for example, 1.5 millimeters thick and constructed of a 90% polished copper exterior and a 10% stainless-steel interior. They heat evenly; are immediately responsive to heat adjustments; and work on gas, electric, and ceramic cooktops.

The pans partners with a copper kettle on the stove in this Portland manse by Jessica Helgerson.

The copper treasures do, however, require care. They’re not nonstick pots and pans, so you need a little oil or butter to get any slip. They’re hand-wash only, and Mauviel advises against using them for long stretches on high heat or leaving them empty on a hot burner. I don’t polish mine, simply because I don’t own any copper polish. The wear demonstrates quickly, and I like that, though if AD were shooting my house, maybe I’d like it less.

Sources indicate that the Black Friday markdowns run across the line: my copper fry pan is going for $280 in the 10-inch size (25% off), a 2.5-quart sauce pan is $450 (29% off), and a 15-piece cookware set is $3,000 (32% off). For anyone who cooks every day, it’s a hard gift to beat. I, for one, now can’t imagine frying my eggs any other way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

According to recent reports, the second major trucking deal between Facebook parent manufacturer Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 new battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”.

Meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This fresh Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The company adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”.

#99018. Michelle Yeoh on Strength, Stunts, and What Makes Us Human

Michelle Yeoh on Strength, Stunts, and What Makes Us Human

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an action hero used to have to be substantial and brawny and brusque.
  • Starring as Olwen, a bioengineered artificial human (or “replicant,” as they’re called in the Blade Runner universe, which includes the new series Blade Runner 2099, out November 25 on Amazon Prime Video), the 64-year-old global megastar literally wrestles with people and replicants alike on-screen.
  • Industry observers note that but in real life, she dances with even larger issues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an action hero used to have to be substantial and brawny and brusque. Michelle Yeoh is none of those things—but you feel her presence and power the instant you meet her. She is kind, warm, and lovely, but she’s also intense…in a really good way. This is a person who listens closely yet also seems ready to launch into a wheelhouse kick at any moment.

Starring as Olwen, a bioengineered artificial human (or “replicant,” as they’re called in the Blade Runner universe, which includes the new series Blade Runner 2099, out November 25 on Amazon Prime Video), the 64-year-old global megastar literally wrestles with people and replicants alike on-screen.

Industry observers note that but in real life, she dances with even larger issues. Like what separates humans from the bot world, how we define strength beyond the physical, why we all need to stretch every morning, and, finally, how she gets over a very specific fear. (If you’ve ever watched her in movies like Tomorrow Never Dies or even Everything Everywhere All At Once, you’ll understand how shocking this particular fear is for her. The solution is one six-letter word…and you’ll just have to read on to find out what that is.).

I sat down with Michelle—who is classically trained in ballet and does many of her own martial arts stunts—in NYC for a wide-ranging convo that starts with robots and ends with what she calls the “Michelle prayer.”.

Women’s Health: What was it like to play a replicant, and how did you think about preparing and training for that mindset?

Michelle Yeoh: We have a brilliant writer, Silka Luisa, who had thought out the story for Blade Runner 2099 [a continuation of the original series] and where it has gone. All these replicants are now in charge of a Los Angeles that is no longer what we know. But it’s very interesting because [the question that arises is] What is humanity? The replicants do give the humans hope. As long as you’re good, as long as you do things the way we want them to be handled, you could go to a better place, because now Los Angeles is not exactly the most habitable place.

It has been revealed that replicants are made to look human. In fact, they are flesh and blood, except they’re stronger, faster. They are able to withstand the new worlds. But empathy is what gives you away as a human. Replicants are born without that emotion. They’re born with memories. They’re given memories to keep them sort of happy and at peace with what they are. Are you born with humanity or does it come with experience and as you live your life with compassion and kindness?

WH: You said that you’re excited for people to see the series and to share ideas and to talk about it. Is that why? The humanity complexity?

Industry observers note that michelle: The worst is they say, “Oh, yeah, it was interesting.…” What is “just” interesting? Hopefully you go home, you think about it, and then you come back and the next day at work or in school, you’re chatting with your friends— “Well, what are you? A replicant or a human? What would you rather be?”.

WH: How did you prepare, physically, for this role?

In a recent development, michelle: I think the older you get, the more you have to do to keep up your muscle strength, to keep your muscles there. Without that, you start walking differently. I have the advantage of understanding my body a lot more because I’ve been doing this for the last, well, ever since I was born. I was dancing, doing sports, everything. I do core-strengthening exercises and tai chi every day.

Recent findings suggest that the core was the most important part of the training because we wanted to nail the way Olwen moved. It was with precision. Because if you want to move with motivation, it has to have that strength, that inner strength, rather than just speed. So when you move, it’s almost like you glide. As a replicant, all the moves are sharp, precise, because they’re so strong and powerful. Actually, when you take a human down, it’s too easy. I think all exercises are core-focused. You can’t lift weights or do pilates without working on the core first. Everything has to start from there.

It has been revealed that WH: Has your own relationship to risk changed over the years? Are there stunts that you used to do in your 30s that now you’re like “nah,” or do you actually feel more powerful and in control?

Michelle: I think that’s really interesting and a good way of putting it. Feeling powerful doesn’t mean being reckless and silly. I feel more powerful in the sense that I have a better assessment of the risk factors. But naturally, because when I was in my 20s, when I first started out, you’re brave and foolish and you’re also so fit. And I was really, really, really fit at that time because I didn’t have any crazy injuries. And, so, fearless is a good word, but fearless and stupid is not good. That’s a bad combination.

In a recent development, sometimes the smallest stunts are the worst because you think they’re easy, and then you don’t pay full attention. You’re not focused enough. You’re focused, but you’re like, “Yeah, yeah, yeah. I’ll get it done.” And that’s when something bad will happen.

In the past, when you are beginning, you listen and you do what they tell you to do, and then you have a lot to prove because you don’t want them to think that you’re unable or you’re not capable, so you do it. But now you go, “How about we…” And then you can speak with power because you know your character. And then I’ll go, “But Olwen won’t do it like that.” And who is going to challenge me?

WH: I understand that you became a bit of a mentor to Hunter Schafer. So talk to us a little about the stunt piece.… Did you help her figure out how to have that voice for herself?

Industry observers note that michelle: To be honest, when I look at her, I go, “Oh my god, I see my young self.” When they show her something, she’ll just throw herself into it because she wants to do it. She’s eager to do it. But then I have to keep reminding her, “You don’t have the same kind of training the stunt people have. So when you can’t do it, it doesn’t mean that you’re not good.”.

It has been revealed that what I do is try to remind her, like, “Hunter, knee pads, Hunter, elbow pads. What is the stunt that you’re doing? Get them on.” Because sometimes you go, like, No, no, no, it’s okay. It’s not okay. Get it on.

It’s a joy to work with her. It’s just a joy to be with her, which sometimes can be difficult because we’re supposed to be against each other in Blade Runner 2099. I mean, she’s a human pretending to be a replicant, pretending to be a blade runner. But somehow their missions intertwine, so they have no choice but to learn to work together. So we have a lot of fun.

Recent findings suggest that WH: What are your nonnegotiables? What are the things you, Michelle, must do every single day for your health that you are consistent with?

Michelle: Water, sunblock, and a lot of stretching. That is a must.

I do tai chi, I do my ballet and tai chi. I’ve been doing that for a long time now. I try to do that every day because I’ve unfortunately had injuries in the past—my back, my knees, my shoulder. I don’t know where I don’t have an injury. As I’m in bed, I do a lot of stretching. When I wake up, the first thing I do in my bed is to go through the motions so that the body wakes up with the mind and everything comes into place.

Recent findings suggest that I think that’s what you have to find: your own moves [or routine] so that you don’t give yourself an excuse when you go, “Oh, it’s raining. No time to go to the gym.” So you just do it even in the bed, you’re stretching, you’re doing all those core exercises to wake up the mind, to wake up the abs, the back, and the legs, everything. And that helps when we’re actually on-set because then I can step into it and know I am strong and ready to go.

I love being outside, going on hikes. Then if I can’t do that, I’m on the elliptical, because I think cardio is still very important. But now, with time, I do a lot more weights. I’m picking up dumbbells or water bottles, whatever works. You have to combine the strengthening of muscles with cardio exercise.

WH: I’m curious if there’s something that is better now in your 60s than it was in your 20s—anything?

Michelle: I think the only thing that’s a little bit better might be this up here [motions to head].

I do a fairly decent job at keeping up the energy, keeping up the spirits, because I also think it’s the inner strength that is very notable. Your mind is very important. If you don’t have the inner peace, it’s very hard to keep control of your body because negative vibes are the worst thing for any human being. When you have negative vibes around you, in you, then you’re down. I honestly believe that because you’ve gone through so many experiences, you’re better for it. I wouldn’t give that up.

Michelle: I have a fear of heights. I know. See, I’m claustrophobic and have a fear of heights.

Michelle: But the magic word is action. Camera rolling…action. And I am focused. Fearless. It’s really, really bizarre. If I don’t hear the word action, then it’s a no go. If I’m in the mall, you know, sometimes you have those walkways that look over the first floor. I walk right in the middle of those. I’m taking no risk. But once action is remarked on set, I’m good.

In a recent development, WH: You mentioned a mantra. What, exactly, is it?

In a recent development, michelle: When I wake up, even before opening my eyes and stretching, I sort of have my own little mantra to wake myself up. I try to talk to my body, thank my body, apologize for anything I’ve done bad, and then welcome everything that’s good because I’m deserving of it.

I don’t sit there and meditate. I don’t understand that at all. Just as long as you feel it yourself that I have what I need for me…because everybody is different.

And that’s why I start my day with a prayer, a mantra. I guess you could call it my own Michelle prayer. Be thankful and be willing to accept anything good that comes your way. I think we have to look at ourselves and have self-worth because I think the inner strength, the inner peace, that sense of compassion and kindness and contentment, is very crucial. Because if you’re always wanting, needing, and thinking about something else, someone else, then you’re always in conflict, first of all, with yourself.

In a recent development, WH: What does the word strength mean to you? When you hear that word, what’s the definition that comes to mind?

Michelle: I think when you hear that word, first of all, it’s always very top layer. You walk into the gym, I have strength, I have power. I put on a power suit. That’s powerful. But for me, true strength is right in there [points to heart]. Showing weakness is strength. Doing a lot of things that people don’t understand, but for you, when you make a choice, it’s strength. There are so many ways of looking at it, and I don’t think there’s one definition unless you check the encyclopedia and they tell you what it is.

WH: And then we’ll just ignore that and go with the Michelle Yeoh definition anyway.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2051 w)

Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase.
  • Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.
  • LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the manufacturer has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The newly introduced S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

It has been revealed that the other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Recent findings suggest that perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re substantial, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

It has been revealed that the clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

There’s an vital caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T claims it is at the moment fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a tech giant to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

Sources indicate that the analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

Sources indicate that I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The manufacturer showed off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The manufacturer also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha revealed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s fresh compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The tech giant revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The upcoming Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company demonstrated off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push latest tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the tech giant has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

According to recent reports, with its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely newly introduced types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no unveiled production prepares, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa demonstrated off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A newly introduced Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

It has been revealed that the e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

#99011. Can You Lose 10 Pounds In A Month? Experts Share 15 Tips For Safe Weight Loss In 30 Days

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1737 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Can You Lose 10 Pounds In A Month? Experts Share 15 Tips For Safe Weight Loss In 30 Days

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it only makes sense to want to give your weight loss journey everything you’ve got.
  • Here's the truth: The average person cannot safely lose 10 pounds in a month, states Michael Glickman, MD, a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness.
  • Meet the experts: Michael Glickman, MD, is a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it only makes sense to want to give your weight loss journey everything you’ve got. And, if you’re into major goals, you may wonder if it’s safe to lose 10 pounds in a month.

Here's the truth: The average person cannot safely lose 10 pounds in a month, states Michael Glickman, MD, a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness. Losing weight at this aggressive of a pace can raise your risk of developing gallstones (painful deposits of digestive fluid in the gallbladder) and up the odds that you’ll regain the weight down the line, he says. (Neither of those are ideal!).

Meet the experts: Michael Glickman, MD, is a board-certified family medicine and obesity medicine physician and founder of Revolution Medicine, Health and Fitness. Michael Hamlin, CSCS, is a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness.

Industry observers note that of course, everyone is different and a lot depends on your starting weight. Also, you can still have aggressive goals when it comes to weight loss—it’s just that 10 pounds in a too-short timeframe is a tricky benchmark for most people. So, how much weight can you safely lose in a month—and how should you even go about it? Here’s what experts suggest.

According to recent reports, the timeline will be different for everyone, given factors like starting weight, genetics, nutrition, activity level, stress, and more. But Dr. Glickman indicates to give yourself anywhere from two to three months to hit that 10-pounds-lost goal. “For some, this could take longer, so be compassionate with your body and prioritize what’s best for your health,” he says.

Sources indicate that when it comes to how much weight is safe to lose at a given time, stick to one to two pounds per week, notes Dr. Glickman. “Some people can shed weight more rapidly in the first month after instituting a lower calorie and healthy diet, however much of the weight loss on the scale will have been due to water weight.”.

If you have obesity and are revamping your eating habits, along with starting an exercise program after being fairly sedentary, you may see bigger gains early on than someone with a lower starting weight who isn’t making drastic changes.

In a recent development, first things first: A safe way to lose weight is a holistic and multi-factorial approach that involves optimal nutrition, frequent exercise, stress reduction, and adequate sleep, claims Dr. Glickman. It's not necessarily about eating less but being conscious of the diversity of plants in your diet, and the avoidance of processed foods, refined oils, and refined carbohydrates, he explains.

On top of that, apply sustainable healthy changes to your routine that you enjoy, states Michael Hamlin, CSCS, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and the founder of Everflex Fitness. Maybe that means attending a workout class with friends twice a week, cooking a plant-based dinner with your partner, or throwing on your favorite podcast and going for a solo walk.

Sleep deprivation promotes an increase in ghrelin, your hunger hormone, which can trigger late night snacking, ultimately increasing your daily caloric intake, says Dr. Glickman. So do your best to get seven to nine hours of sleep per night. Not only that, getting more sleep helps you feel more energized, so you can add more activity to your day.

In a recent development, it may sound simple, but 30 minutes of daily walking can do wonders, states Dr. Glickman. “It isn’t about calorie burning—it’s about the mobility, the happy hormones your brain releases, and the physiological anti-inflammatory responses that have long-term impacts on your weight.”.

Getting daily steps in has health benefits ranging from lowering your risk of developing type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease to helping you live longer. While any movement is good, moving at a brisk pace is the best way to get in all those extra perks.

Recent findings suggest that plant diversity has been shown to have the most beneficial impact on the gut microbiome, which influences your metabolic set point (the body’s preferred weight), insulin levels, and fat storage, notes Dr. Glickman. Plant-based diets are also linked to a lower risk of developing heart disease, stroke, and diabetes, making this a significant win for your overall health, too.

His suggestion? Try a plant-based day or meal per week to ensure you’re supporting your gut microbiome and loading up on the veggies.

It’s best to consult a doctor or registered dietitian to determine your daily caloric needs since it depends on your age, gender, activity level, muscle mass, current weight, and the amount of calories you burn at rest (a.k.a. your basal metabolic rate), claims Hamlin. From there, they can determine a slight calorie deficit, or how many calories you need in a day to lose one to two pounds a week, he explains.

Recent findings suggest that while you’re waiting for a consult, check out the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases’ online body weight planner. It asks you to enter some basic information like your current weight, your ideal weight, and your activity level, and provides what your daily calorie goals should be to help you get there.

“Stress can lead to increased hunger hormones and an elevated metabolic set point,” indicates Dr. Glickman. Higher levels of the stress hormone cortisol can create stubborn fat distribution around the abdomen, he adds.

It has been revealed that although this one is often easier said than done, to help combat stress and anxiety, try relaxation techniques like meditation, yoga, and journaling. And, of course, if you’re struggling with stress management, consider reaching out to a mental health therapist for individual guidance on navigating everything.

“Sometimes we can mistake the feeling of thirst for hunger, so make sure to stay hydrated throughout the day, especially during and after exercise,” Dr. Glickman says. Women should drink about 11.5 cups (2.7 liters) of fluids a day, per Mayo Clinic. (Note: That total can come from food and liquids.).

It has been revealed that strength training has a significant impact on your metabolism and fat burning capabilities, studies show, so incorporate resistance training at least three days a week, notes Dr. Glickman. Just take note that because strength training builds muscle, you may notice little or even no overall weight change at times, even though you are losing fat. (Not sure where to start with your strength training journey? Try Women's Health's The Woman's Guide To Strength Training: Dumbbells.).

HIIT workouts burn a ton of calories and can change your body composition while building muscle, says Hamlin. In fact, women who incorporated HIIT programming achieved similar body composition and aerobic capacity results in half the time as women who did moderate-intensity workouts, a 2017 study published in the Journal of Diabetes Research found.

Recent findings suggest that fiber helps regulate blood sugar levels, prevent insulin resistance and diabetes, and is an excellent source of nutrition for healthy bacteria in the gut, indicates Dr. Glickman. High-fiber foods like vegetables are also filling without overloading on the calories, explains Hamlin. You can get fiber in powder or supplement form, but your best (and healthiest) bet is from plants, adds Dr. Glickman.

Weight gain is linked with the consumption of highly processed and packaged foods, Dr. Glickman claims. “This includes any food item in a wrapper with ingredients you can’t pronounce, even if the calories and carbohydrates seem appealing,” he explains. “Always choose whole foods over packaged ones.”.

Do your best to prioritize cooking at home to eliminate sneaky fats, sugars, and processed ingredients that are not listed on a menu, claims Dr. Glickman.

Focus on the quality of food on your plate and aim for three hearty meals a day that include a small amount of complex carbohydrates (root veggies and whole grains), a moderate amount of high-quality protein (fish, chicken, eggs, and tofu), and lots of plant-based fiber, indicates Dr. Glickman.

Alcoholic drinks lack nutritional value and are usually packed with calories, so it’s best to scale back on booze, claims Hamlin. When you drink alcohol, it also immediately goes to the liver where it’s prioritized as an energy source, so your body burns alcohol cals first. Not only that, alcohol also lowers your inhibitions and raises the odds you’ll eat more than you need to feel satiated.

To help with accountability, Hamlin suggests using a food journal or app to track your meals. This will give you a better understanding and awareness of how many calories you’re consuming and at which meal. Research indicates this is an effective way to lose weight, too. One study found that people who tracked their meals at least five days of each week had “significant and sustained weight loss” over time compared to people who tracked less or inconsistently.

It can take time for your stomach to recognize when it’s full, so pause in between portions before deciding if you actually want more, claims Hamlin. You can either pre-pack your meals with smaller portion sizes or use smaller plates to provide a visual cue. One scientific analysis of 14 studies found that people who ate smaller portions had a “substantial” drop in how many calories they ate each day.

Think long-term about weight loss and establish a goal that is realistic for your lifestyle, says Hamlin. Your goals might take time and patience, but that’s okay, he adds. “Weight loss isn't solely about a caloric deficit, because the body is a super complex piece of machinery, and we can't simply boil all of weight loss down to calories in versus calories out.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.
  • It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.
  • Sources indicate that hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Sources indicate that hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the new Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

According to recent reports, hyundai noted the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car).

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

It has been revealed that while earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

It has been revealed that the updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s upcoming Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the fresh Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

15 Best Places to Buy Bedding, Editor Picks (2026)

📅 12 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use.
  • Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand.
  • Sources indicate that for bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use. Every retailer here comes recommended by an AD editor or contributor who has lived with the bedding at home for a long stretch: flannel kept on the bed through May, linen hauled to a communal laundromat and back, or a sheet set that survives a dog digging in every night.

Each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand. Rest assured: they’re all comfy.

Sources indicate that for bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop. Its European Linen Sheet Set earned our pick for the best affordable linen sheets, and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker has recently added the brand to her list of favorites. “The price point is unbeatable, and I love that they offer bedding sets in beautiful colorways and a variety of fabric options,” she notes. “The quality is also impressive, especially considering the affordability.”.

It has been revealed that made from 100% European flax, the sheets cost a fraction of what competitors charge, thanks in part to Quince’s direct-to-consumer model which skips traditional retail markups. “I love its airy nature along with the gorgeous Bordeaux color that complements the rest of my decor,” says Baker. The bedding range extends to quilts and coverlets, , and the brand’s down comforter also made our ranking of the best comforters.

Industry observers note that anyone who has paused a Nancy Meyers movie to study the bedroom should start with Serena & Lily. The brand is based in Sausalito, California, but its textured, breezy bedding and decor would look right at home on any coast, Nantucket included. The range covers lightweight linen and crisp cotton percale in pale colors and easygoing prints.

In a recent development, of all the bedding Baker has tested, the Nantucket Stripe Sheet Set ranks near the top for its light weight and “worn-in texture,” which keeps the linen soft instead of scratchy. The ruffle trim keeps her bed from looking too plain. “The striped mink print does give a seaside vibe, but it’s been neutral enough to layer with any color bed cover without clashing with the rest of my minimal, romantic decor over the few months I’ve tested the set,” she adds. For a top layer, there’s the scalloped Baywood Quilt, which Alpert likes as a light blanket for “when you want to throw something over while you read your favorite Emily Henry book in bed.”.

Industry observers note that boll & Branch sheets arrive feeling as if they’ve already been through several wash cycles, without the fraying or pilling that usually comes with that. Contributor Rachel Fletcher tested the brand’s percale, Supima cotton, flannel, and linen, but its signature sateen stood out most for its long-staple cotton and a soft, smooth finish. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, make them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” she states. Converts can outfit the rest of the room too, with Boll & Branch’s mattresses and bedroom furniture.

In a recent development, brooklinen started out selling two things, cotton percale and sateen sheets, and has since added cashmere, brushed flannel, and a long list of prints. Pieces come in bundled sets or one at a time, and prices land between the budget brands and the luxury labels. Our editors keep coming back to the linen sheets, which they use in every season.

“Since I don’t live my life on a Greek island, I thought white linen sheets year-round might be a slightly bold move, but the nature of the fiber is versatile and temperature regulating,” indicates AD contributor Madeleine Luckel, who tested the Core Sheet Set. Fletcher sleeps on the Luxe Sheet Set and credits it with keeping her cool. “I’m a hot sleeper with sensitive skin, and they’re really cool on my skin at night, which is a huge relief,” she says. “I love the breathability of these sheets.”.

Recent findings suggest that few bedding brands have tied their name to sustainability as closely as Coyuchi. Its linen sheets are made from certified organic French flax grown without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, and the brand also offers percale, sateen, and flannel sheets. The earthy color palette is a selling point on its own.

In a recent development, “I love the color, which is what drew me to these sheets in the first place,” says Sam Cochran, global features editor. “They’re the perfect brown—a tad auburn, ever so slightly timeworn in palette.”.

Shopping writer Julia Harrison and contributor Kate McGregor agree: Garnet Hill is their “secret spot” for bedding. Harrison is devoted to the flannel sheets and admits she leaves them on the bed through May because “they’re so soft, I’d rather suffer in my own sweat than switch them out.” The ticking stripe is “perfectly classic—like a true vintage piece, but not actually vintage…that might be tough sell in the bedding department.” Alpert also loves her flannel pick, a duvet cover that “signals a cottagecore moment without going over the top.” Paired with her Ostermoor duvet insert, it’s “like climbing under a layer of meringue.” Garnet Hill specializes in vintage-inspired designs, patchwork quilts especially, made in 100% linen and 100% cotton options at reasonable prices.

Cozy Earth makes breathable bedding for people who run hot at night, and its signature bamboo bedding, made of 100% viscose, are the brand’s best-known example. “I honestly thought these sheets were silk,” notes contributor Megan Wahn. “That’s how smooth and soft they feel.” Wahn tested them mostly in winter, and despite feeling cool to the touch, they kept her warm. “I’m especially eager to see how they perform in the summer,” she adds. “Something about their smoothness makes me think the summer-night sweats won’t stand a chance.”.

Industry observers note that parachute is where we send anyone after classic, well-made cotton bedding. Its sets and bundles are designed with sustainability in mind, and the percale and brushed cotton are made by artisans at the brand’s factory in Portugal.

“We love [Parachute] because the bedding is designed to provide a hotel-like experience, offering a perfect balance of softness and crispness,” claims Stephanie Kraus of Stephanie Kraus Designs, whose clients favor the brand’s linen bedding sets. “They become softer with each wash while maintaining their durability and are super soft to sleep in every night.”.

Fletcher also praises the brand’s commitment to organic, ethically sourced materials; the Organic Cloud Cotton Duvet Set, for one, is made of Oeko-Tex-certified 100% cotton. “I try a lot of bedding in this line of work and the more I do, the more I appreciate ethical and organic production, even if the price tag is a little higher,” she says.

Industry observers note that greenRow makes charming, long-lasting bedding from recycled and sustainably sourced materials, and it has won over several people on the Shop AD team. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls the Helena Floral Sheet Set “without a doubt, the softest sheets I own.” She compares the cotton satin to velvet, and the butter-yellow florals and green micro-gingham ruffle make the set prettier still. McGregor, meanwhile, is partial to the reversible patchwork quilt. “It’s the kind of blanket that feels substantial without trapping heat or feeling stuffy,” she notes. “I feel cocooned without a down comforter, but I’m not smothered when I sleep sans AC in the warmer months. It’s a year-round bedding piece for me, especially since the color palette can lean moodier or more cheerful depending on my sheet selection.”.

Rebecca Udall is a newer name and one worth knowing. Her namesake bedding line is built on romantic, careful details, such as soft-colored decorative embroidery along the sheets. McGregor’s current favorite is this scalloped percale sheet set. “The feel is like a washed percale, crisp but forgiving, and I find that the subtle color on the detailed edge gives the perfect amount of visual interest to my all-white bedscape,” she notes. If you want less ornament, try the Georgiana duvet cover, with faint ladderstitch detailing hand-embroidered by artisans in Northern Italy.

It has been revealed that hommey, an Australian brand founded in 2020, first caught on with its boldly striped robes and nightwear. It has since carried those designs into cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers. Across both fabrics, there are more than two dozen colors and prints to choose from. For maximalists who want to try color-blocking, the brand’s bolder colorways are a great place to start.

Baker tested the brown sugar linen duvet cover and found the stonewashed, Oeko-Tex certified flax smoother and more broken-in straight out of the package than the Quince version she already owned (above). “I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes,” Baker says. She pairs the chocolatey shade with burgundy linen sheets for a moodier bed, though it also works as a neutral with lighter sheets in oatmeal, which pick up the cream trim. The one drawback is that the cover has no interior ties, so the insert can shift around inside.

Industry observers note that australian brand Cultiver makes linen sheets and duvets with an easy, beachy look. Its Oeko-Tex certified pieces are an investment, and a worthwhile one. Coverlets are generously sized so they drape loosely, and the envelope-back pillow cases hold their shape without looking stiff. Fletcher has put her set through heavy use and many wash cycles. “Linen is my bedding fabric of choice pretty much 365 days a year, and Cultiver’s high-quality sheet sets do it for me in a way no other brand has. Out of all the sets I’ve tried, this one has stood the test of many washes, my dog digging in them to get cozy at night, and surviving across seasons without feeling worn or threadbare,” she states.

According to recent reports, erica Tanov’s bedding is handmade by artisans in Jaipur, in 100% linen with embroidery drawn from traditional Indian textiles. Harrison calls hers “a lifetime set” that “draws more compliments than anything else in my apartment.” The linen is soft and tough: She hauls this sheet set to her neighborhood laundromat, and it survives the communal machines without damage. It’s the first linen set she’s found to be “city-friendly,” as she calls it. She hasn’t tried the quilts or throw blankets yet, though one already tops her birthday wishlist (this one).

Industry observers note that it depends mostly on how you like your bed to feel and how reliable your thermostat is. If you like the crisp coolness of hotel sheets, try percale. If you like a soft, organic feel, try linen for a breezy texture, or bamboo sheets for something similar to silk. Cotton sheets (like Supima sets) are often the most durable over time, especially after many, many washes. Your warmest options are generally flannel sets, and your coolest are generally bamboo and percale. For a basic setup, we recommend a full sheet set (flat sheet included, people) plus a duvet insert with a cover. The cover protects the insert and keeps it clean, so you’ll generally only need to wash the insert every six months rather than weekly like your sheets. Harrison likes to go one step further with a bed blanket underneath her duvet and above her sheets for a bit of weight and additional warmth. If a fluffy duvet isn’t your thing, a quilt or coverlet can take its place and add a little more weight.

What to Look for When Buying Bedding.

Sources indicate that start with the fiber content on the label. Search for 100% cotton, linen (the more organic, the better), and steer clear of polyesters or more plastic fibers, as they’re likely to pill more promptly and break apart in the washer and dryer.

Latest Update: Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.
  • Industry observers note that the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected.
  • Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

Industry observers note that the Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.

A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

It has been revealed that on November 6, the same day Elon Musk revealed the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

According to recent reports, newly introduced inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search indicated no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

In a recent development, if there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

It has been revealed that but the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”.

That’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

Sources indicate that some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t mentioned whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

This is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

It has been revealed that I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we mentioned it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

Industry observers note that if you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper latest option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.
